title: Softmax Routing Dynamics in Mixture-of-Experts Models:Collapse and Recovery

paper.title: Softmax Routing Dynamics in Mixture-of-Experts Models: Collapse and Recovery
paper.abstract: Abstract Softmax routing in mixture-of-experts models can concentrate probability on a subset of experts, suppressing access to the others. We study how this concentration forms, why it persists, and how suppressed probabilities recover. For fixed experts, a stationary-loss barrier identifies the face supporting the optimal routed output. In a common-target square-loss model with freely trainable expert outputs, slow adaptation tracks fixed-expert dynamics on finite horizons, while every fixed positive adaptation rate yields an interior routing limit. An exact normal-velocity decomposition separates complementary-expert covariance from relative gradient advantage. Under positive two-sided power bounds along recovery paths, uniform over initial masses, the resulting coefficient’s order of vanishing gives logarithmic or power-law recovery times. Integrations of constructed fields reproduce these orders. An exact discrete log-odds identity relates neural updates to threshold crossing. In paired Transformer-MoE training, removing a class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays confirmed recovery and reduces accumulated log-odds on fixed tokens, both with and without capacity constraints.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models increase capacity by activating only a subset of expert subnetworks for each input, enabling conditional computation at large scale [ 36 , 23 , 13 , 12 ] . A learned router assigns probabilities to experts, while top- k k selection and capacity constraints determine the executed assignments. During training, self-reinforcing routing preferences can concentrate assignments on a few experts, a form of routing collapse [ 36 , 9 ] . We study routing concentration : small pre-dispatch probability mass outside a proper coordinate face. Asymptotic concentration means that this mass tends to zero. Severe concentration suppresses access to some experts for a given input and constitutes the probability-space aspect of routing collapse . Finite logits keep probabilities positive, so finite-time collapse appears as near-boundary concentration. We call the return of a suppressed probability to a prescribed positive threshold recovery . Load-balancing losses encourage balanced aggregate expert use [ 36 , 13 , 47 ] . Yet individual inputs can concentrate on different experts while maintaining balanced aggregate loads. Routing probabilities also evolve jointly with expert parameters and input representations. Persistent concentration and subsequent reactivation observed during MoE training [ 35 ] therefore raise three questions: which simplex face is selected as routing concentrates? Why can concentration persist when experts are trainable? What determines the time required for a suppressed expert to recover? Near a simplex boundary, a small probability can respond slowly even to a favorable gradient signal. Continuous-time gradient flow on softmax logits makes this effect explicit. For a routing vector p p , let J ⁡ ( p ) = diag ⁡ ( p ) − p ​ p ⊤ J(p)=\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^{\top} be the softmax Jacobian and g g the probability gradient of the half-loss. Euclidean logit-gradient flow and its probability-space form are q ˙ = − J ⁡ ( p ) ​ g , p ˙ = − J ​ ( p ) 2 ​ g . \dot{q}=-J(p)g,\qquad\dot{p}=-J(p)^{2}g. At p j = 0 p_{j}=0 , the j j th row of J ⁡ ( p ) J(p) vanishes. Under bounded gradient signals, normal probability motion therefore vanishes as p j ↓ 0 p_{j}\downarrow 0 ; we call this boundary degeneracy . It is a property of the vector field, whereas concentration describes the routing state. The direction and order of normal motion depend on the complementary routing state and gradient field. Related Jacobian structures appear in value–softmax dynamics [ 37 ] ; here we characterize how this geometry governs routing concentration, persistence, and recovery.

sections.heading: Main results
sections.text: For fixed experts, the optimal routed output is the target’s projection onto the expert convex hull. Below the smallest suboptimal stationary loss, every limit point represents this projection and is supported on experts in the minimal hull face containing it. Geometric separation gives bounds on outside-face mass and neighborhood entry times ( Section 3 ). Expert adaptation introduces a second time scale. As the expert-update rate tends to zero, the joint flow approaches the fixed-expert trajectory on each fixed finite horizon. For every fixed positive rate in the common-target square-loss model with freely trainable outputs, however, residual decay makes the logits converge to finite limits and routing to an interior point. Thus concentration can persist over finite horizons even though the long-time limit is interior ( Section 4 ). Our main recovery result separates complementary-expert covariance from relative gradient advantage in an exact normal-velocity decomposition ( Section 5 ). For a suppressed probability x = p j x=p_{j} , it gives x ˙ = x ​ ( 1 − x ) 2 ​ Γ j \dot{x}=x(1-x)^{2}\Gamma_{j} . The order of vanishing of Γ j \Gamma_{j} governs the recovery time T θ ​ ( ε ) T_{\theta}(\varepsilon) from initial mass ε \varepsilon to a fixed threshold θ \theta . For fixed α ⩾ 0 \alpha\geqslant 0 , positive two-sided comparisons along the entire recovery path, with constants independent of ε \varepsilon , yield Γ j ≍ x α ⟹ T θ ​ ( ε ) ≍ { log ⁡ ( 1 / ε ) , α = 0 , ε − α , α > 0 , ε ↓ 0 . \Gamma_{j}\asymp x^{\alpha}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T_{\theta}(\varepsilon)\asymp\begin{cases}\log(1/\varepsilon),&\alpha=0,\\ \varepsilon^{-\alpha},&\alpha>0,\end{cases}\qquad\varepsilon\downarrow 0. For two experts under the same advantage signal bounded above and away from zero, squared-Jacobian, single-Jacobian, and Euclidean projected flows yield inverse-probability, logarithmic, and bounded recovery times, respectively. For input-conditioned routers, an affine separation criterion describes initial routing differences, and an exact discrete log-odds identity relates threshold crossing to individual neural updates ( Section 6 ). Paired Transformer-MoE interventions show that removing a class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays confirmed recovery and reduces accumulated log-odds on fixed tokens, both with and without capacity constraints ( Section 7 ). sections.heading: Routing, allocation, and statistical recovery
sections.text: Learned gating originated in adaptive and hierarchical mixtures [ 19 , 20 ] . Modern methods study expert assignment, balanced utilization, expert choice, and differentiable dispatch [ 24 , 45 , 17 , 31 , 40 ] . Expert-wise biases control aggregate loads [ 38 ] , and assignment dynamics admit primal–dual formulations [ 16 ] . Load balance, input specialization, and token-level route quality are distinct allocation properties [ 15 , 39 , 43 ] ; assignments can become established early in pre-training [ 42 ] . Statistical analyses address identifiability and estimation [ 6 , 2 , 28 , 29 ] or recovery of latent clusters and tasks [ 8 , 11 , 21 , 25 ] . Stochastic-optimization analyses quantify how routing sparsity affects overall convergence [ 46 ] . We study the time a suppressed routing probability takes to regain a prescribed threshold during optimization.

sections.heading: Concentration observables and softmax dynamics
sections.text: Representation clustering around expert centroids [ 10 ] , concentration of expert-selection paths across layers [ 14 ] , and the effective rank of routing-similarity graphs across reasoning rollouts [ 7 ] describe observables distinct from our outside-face mass for an individual probability vector. Optimization geometry determines how gradients move that vector: replicator dynamics and entropic mirror descent induce a single softmax Jacobian in probability space [ 18 , 34 , 5 ] , whereas Euclidean logit-gradient flow induces its square. Tabular softmax policy-optimization rates depend on initialization and bounds on optimal-action probabilities [ 26 ] . Face selection also relates to active-set identification [ 41 ] . Our stationary-loss barrier combines convex projection and loss dissipation to identify the hull face supporting the limiting output; exposing directions then control outside-face mass.

sections.heading: Trainable value–softmax dynamics
sections.text: Varre, Rofin, and Flammarion [ 37 ] study joint value–softmax flow. Their square-loss analysis gives exponential residual decay and finite cumulative polarization; the latter is derived under a zero-initialized value matrix. We use the same dissipation mechanism to establish convergence of logits and expert outputs for arbitrary finite initialization and every positive expert-update rate, with explicit tail and probability-floor bounds ( Theorem 4.2 ). Combining this result with the slow-expert approximation separates finite-horizon concentration from the interior long-time limit. Recovery is then governed by the normal coefficient in Section 5 .

sections.heading: Router–expert coupling
sections.text: Joint training couples routing preferences to expert adaptation. Kiselev [ 22 ] derives symmetry-breaking bifurcations in a two-expert reinforcement-and-decay model. Ahrac, Hochwald, and Geva [ 1 ] analyze shared token directions in router and expert gradients and the effects of load balancing on their alignment. We study how a class-conditional target–comparator gradient contrast affects subsequent recovery. Matched neural branches estimate the response to removing this contrast, and the discrete log-odds identity relates the observed routing changes to individual threshold crossing.

sections.heading: 8 Discussion and conclusions
sections.text: The normal-velocity decomposition isolates two effects: covariance among complementary experts and the suppressed route’s relative gradient advantage. Their combined coefficient distinguishes recovery regimes within the same squared-Jacobian geometry. Positive two-sided power bounds along recovery paths, uniform over initial masses, give logarithmic or power-law recovery times; constructed fields reproduce these orders. Face selection and expert adaptation determine the setting in which recovery takes place. A stationary-loss barrier identifies the supporting face for fixed experts. In the common-target square-loss model with freely trainable outputs, slow adaptation approximates fixed-expert trajectories on finite horizons, while every fixed positive rate gives an interior limit. Explicit tails and probability floors quantify the interior convergence for each fixed rate. In paired Transformer-MoE training, removing a class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays confirmed recovery and reduces accumulated log-odds on fixed tokens under both dispatch policies. These intervention effects connect a change in training gradients to the motion needed for recovery. The discrete log-odds identity relates the token-level response to threshold crossing under the actual optimizer updates. Estimating recovery coefficients in naturally evolving systems and testing their predictions on new trajectories would extend the continuous analysis. Independent evaluation inputs and norm-matched gradient controls would further assess how the neural response transfers across inputs and depends on the chosen gradient direction.

We study how this concentration forms, why it persists, and how suppressed probabilities recover. For fixed experts, a stationary-loss barrier identifies the face supporting the optimal routed output. In a common-target square-loss model with freely trainable expert outputs, slow adaptation tracks fixed-expert dynamics on finite horizons, while every fixed positive adaptation rate yields an interior routing limit. An exact normal-velocity decomposition separates complementary-expert covariance from relative gradient advantage. Keywords: mixture of experts, softmax routing, routing collapse, gradient flow, routing recovery 1 Introduction Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models increase capacity by activating only a subset of expert subnetworks for each input, enabling conditional computation at large scale [ 36 , 23 , 13 , 12 ] . A learned router assigns probabilities to experts, while top- k k selection and capacity constraints determine the executed assignments. During training, self-reinforcing routing preferences can concentrate assignments on a few experts, a form of routing collapse [ 36 , 9 ] . We study routing concentration : small pre-dispatch probability mass outside a proper coordinate face. Asymptotic concentration means that this mass tends to zero. Severe concentration suppresses access to some experts for a given input and constitutes the probability-space aspect of routing collapse . Finite logits keep probabilities positive, so finite-time collapse appears as near-boundary concentration. We call the return of a suppressed probability to a prescribed positive threshold recovery . Load-balancing losses encourage balanced aggregate expert use [ 36 , 13 , 47 ] . Yet individual inputs can concentrate on different experts while maintaining balanced aggregate loads. Routing probabilities also evolve jointly with expert parameters and input representations. Persistent concentration and subsequent reactivation observed during MoE training [ 35 ] therefore raise three questions: which simplex face is selected as routing concentrates? Why can concentration persist when experts are trainable? What determines the time required for a suppressed expert to recover? Near a simplex boundary, a small probability can respond slowly even to a favorable gradient signal. Continuous-time gradient flow on softmax logits makes this effect explicit. For a routing vector p p , let J ⁡ ( p ) = diag ⁡ ( p ) − p ​ p ⊤ J(p)=\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^{	op} be the softmax Jacobian and g g the probability gradient of the half-loss. Euclidean logit-gradient flow and its probability-space form are q ˙ = − J ⁡ ( p ) ​ g , p ˙ = − J ​ ( p ) 2 ​ g . \dot{q}=-J(p)g,\qquad\dot{p}=-J(p)^{2}g. At p j = 0 p_{j}=0 , the j j th row of J ⁡ ( p ) J(p) vanishes. Under bounded gradient signals, normal probability motion therefore vanishes as p j ↓ 0 p_{j}\downarrow 0 ; we call this boundary degeneracy . It is a property of the vector field, whereas concentration describes the routing state. The direction and order of normal motion depend on the complementary routing state and gradient field. Related Jacobian structures appear in value–softmax dynamics [ 37 ] ; here we characterize how this geometry governs routing concentration, persistence, and recovery. Main results For fixed experts, the optimal routed output is the target’s projection onto the expert convex hull. Below the smallest suboptimal stationary loss, every limit point represents this projection and is supported on experts in the minimal hull face containing it. Geometric separation gives bounds on outside-face mass and neighborhood entry times ( Section 3 ). Expert adaptation introduces a second time scale. As the expert-update rate tends to zero, the joint flow approaches the fixed-expert trajectory on each fixed finite horizon. For every fixed positive rate in the common-target square-loss model with freely trainable outputs, however, residual decay makes the logits converge to finite limits and routing to an interior point. Thus concentration can persist over finite horizons even though the long-time limit is interior ( Section 4 ). Our main recovery result separates complementary-expert covariance from relative gradient advantage in an exact normal-velocity decomposition ( Section 5 ). For a suppressed probability x = p j x=p_{j} , it gives x ˙ = x ​ ( 1 − x ) 2 ​ Γ j \dot{x}=x(1-x)^{2}\Gamma_{j} . Code is available at https://github.com/shengze-xu/softmax-routing-dynamics . 1.1 Related work Routing, allocation, and statistical recovery Learned gating originated in adaptive and hierarchical mixtures [ 19 , 20 ] . Modern methods study expert assignment, balanced utilization, expert choice, and differentiable dispatch [ 24 , 45 , 17 , 31 , 40 ] . Expert-wise biases control aggregate loads [ 38 ] , and assignment dynamics admit primal–dual formulations [ 16 ] . Load balance, input specialization, and token-level route quality are distinct allocation properties [ 15 , 39 , 43 ] ; assignments can become established early in pre-training [ 42 ] . Statistical analyses address identifiability and estimation [ 6 , 2 , 28 , 29 ] or recovery of latent clusters and tasks [ 8 , 11 , 21 , 25 ] . Stochastic-optimization analyses quantify how routing sparsity affects overall convergence [ 46 ] . We study the time a suppressed routing probability takes to regain a prescribed threshold during optimization. Concentration observables and softmax dynamics Representation clustering around expert centroids [ 10 ] , concentration of expert-selection paths across layers [ 14 ] , and the effective rank of routing-similarity graphs across reasoning rollouts [ 7 ] describe observables distinct from our outside-face mass for an individual probability vector. Optimization geometry determines how gradients move that vector: replicator dynamics and entropic mirror descent induce a single softmax Jacobian in probability space [ 18 , 34 , 5 ] , whereas Euclidean logit-gradient flow induces its square. Tabular softmax policy-optimization rates depend on initialization and bounds on optimal-action probabilities [ 26 ] . Face selection also relates to active-set identification [ 41 ] . Our stationary-loss barrier combines convex projection and loss dissipation to identify the hull face supporting the limiting output; exposing directions then control outside-face mass. Trainable value–softmax dynamics Varre, Rofin, and Flammarion [ 37 ] study joint value–softmax flow. Their square-loss analysis gives exponential residual decay and finite cumulative polarization; the latter is derived under a zero-initialized value matrix. We use the same dissipation mechanism to establish convergence of logits and expert outputs for arbitrary finite initialization and every positive expert-update rate, with explicit tail and probability-floor bounds ( Theorem 4.2 ). Combining this result with the slow-expert approximation separates finite-horizon concentration from the interior long-time limit. Recovery is then governed by the normal coefficient in Section 5 . Router–expert coupling Joint training couples routing preferences to expert adaptation. Kiselev [ 22 ] derives symmetry-breaking bifurcations in a two-expert reinforcement-and-decay model. Ahrac, Hochwald, and Geva [ 1 ] analyze shared token directions in router and expert gradients and the effects of load balancing on their alignment. We study how a class-conditional target–comparator gradient contrast affects subsequent recovery.
